1. Dataset at a glance

Each row is a single Lydia card transaction. All transactions are denominated in EUR and all cards are of card_type = lydia-card — those two columns are therefore constant and carry no analytical signal. Member and merchant names look like realistic French-market data (Carrefour, Monoprix, SNCF, Uber, Apple, Netflix, …). Debits are stored as negative values, credits (refunds) as positive. There is a modest ~90-day window.

2. Missing values

columnmissing%
pfm_recurring_frequency7,89997.27%
major_category1231.51%
merchant_name1131.39%
Only three columns have any missing values, and two of them have a known structural cause:
  • pfm_recurring_frequency — 97.3% missing. This is by design: only recurring charges are tagged (and the only non-null value observed is monthly — think Netflix, Spotify, Apple subscriptions). It is a sparse flag, not broken data.
  • major_category — 1.5% missing (123 rows). Every single missing row has status = refunded and minor_category = refund. Refunds are intentionally left uncategorized.
  • merchant_name — 1.4% missing (113 rows). These lack a readable label even though merchant_id is populated. This is a genuine data-quality gap worth filling (e.g. by joining a merchant dimension on merchant_id).

3. Column-by-column analysis

3.1 amount_value & fees

Left: linear histogram clipped to ±€200. The bulk of spend sits between −€50 and 0. Right: log10|amount| shows the long upper tail that linear scaling hides — a clump of transactions beyond 105 EUR (€100k+).

Box plot on log scale. Each dot in the far-right smear is a transaction > ~€1,000; the farthest dots approach €400,000.

Fees are in cents. The stored integer takes only seven distinct non-zero values — 100, 120, 180, 240, 400, 600, 4000 — which after dividing by 100 map to €1.00, €1.20, €1.80, €2.40, €4.00, €6.00, and €40.00. These are a published tariff grid (likely ATM, foreign-exchange, instant-transfer and dispute fees). Only 60 rows (0.7%) carry any fee at all; the remaining 8,061 are fee-free, so means and totals should always exclude the zeros to be meaningful.

3.2 status

98.5% of rows are completed; the remaining 123 (1.5%) are refunded. Refunds are the mirror image of normal transactions: positive amounts, missing major_category, and minor_category = refund.

3.3 major_category & minor_category

Groceries dominate the volume mix (~29%), followed by entertainment (~25%), transportation (~16%) and restaurants (~16%). Finance (ATM withdrawals, cash services) and self-care are small but distinct tails. Note that minor_category = refund is the catch-all bucket for the 123 refunds and the reason major_category appears null in the chart.

3.4 card_name

3.5 digitalization_type

Suspected merchant-name leakage into digitalization_type. The valid-looking values are apple_pay, google_pay, samsung_pay, none, UNKNOWN. But we also see UBER, PAYPAL, GOOGLE_PAYMENTS_INC, SPOTIFY, MICROSOFT_NETWORK, NETFLIX, TAXIFY, STRIPE, DEEZER — those are merchants/payment processors, not wallet types. Something upstream is populating this field from the wrong source for ~275 rows (3.4%).

3.6 pfm_recurring_frequency

Only two observed values: monthly (222 rows, 2.7%) and null (the other 97.3%). Of the monthly-recurring rows, 90% fall under major_category = entertainment — i.e. streaming / app subscriptions.

3.7 Temporal columns

Daily volume is remarkably stable at ~85–100 txns/day over the 90-day window, with a very mild weekend uptick. Hourly distribution peaks in the lunch (12-14h) and evening (17-20h) windows and dips as expected overnight. No visible gaps or load drops in the time series.

3.8 Merchants

The top merchants are consumer staples — Apple billing, McDonald's, Carrefour variants, Uber, Monoprix. Interestingly, there are 2,789 unique merchant_id values but only 959 unique merchant_name values, meaning the same displayed merchant maps to many internal IDs. This is normal for acquiring-processor data (one brand → many terminal/outlet IDs) but should be remembered when aggregating.

4. Deviations & outliers

4.1 Amount-value outliers

Robust statistics for amount_value:

  • Median: €-10.65, IQR: €18.62 (Q1=€-23.35, Q3=€-4.73)
  • Tukey fence (1.5·IQR): [€-51.28, €23.20] — anything outside is a statistical outlier.
  • Median absolute deviation (MAD): €7.64 — more robust than std against the extreme tail.
  • Transactions with |amount_value| > €1,000: 188 rows (2.31% of the dataset).
Clear data-entry / unit errors in the top of the distribution. The 15 largest absolute amounts are all between €158,000 and €399,000 for merchants that cannot plausibly charge those sums (McDonald's, Burger King, Buffalo Grill, Pizza Cosy, Uber Eats). The most likely explanations are a decimal-point error, a currency confusion, or an encoding bug — not real card spend. These rows should be quarantined before any averages, totals, or revenue figures are reported.

4.3 Duplicate ref_id rows

120 ref_id values appear twice, covering 240 rows total. Within each duplicate pair, the member_id, merchant_id, amount_value, created_at and status all match — only the transaction_id differs. This looks like the same real transaction getting ingested twice. If left as-is, every one of these rows would be double-counted in totals.

4.4 Other data-quality flags

  • Constant columns — amount_currency (always EUR) and card_type (always lydia-card) are safe to drop from any model.
  • Mixed units — fees is in cents while amount_value is in euros; any arithmetic that touches both columns must align them first.
  • Casing / language inconsistency in card_name (French and English spellings coexist) and digitalization_type (apple_pay vs UNKNOWN — mixed casing).
  • Merchant name blanks on 113 rows — these should be back-filled via merchant_id.
  • Refund mirror — all 123 refunds are positive amounts, missing major_category. Reporting pipelines should either join refunds to the original transaction or treat minor_category = refund as its own category.
